entities.summary:
Physiology, the scientific study of the functions and mechanisms in living systems, emerged prominently during the Classical Era, particularly in Ancient Greece and Rome, where thinkers like Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) and Galen (c. 129–216 CE) laid foundational principles. Its exploration spanned various cultures and civilizations, influencing not only medicine but also philosophy, ethics, and the understanding of life itself. This field matters profoundly as it bridges the gap between biology and medicine, offering insights that resonate through centuries of scientific inquiry and innovation.

During the Classical period, significant milestones in physiology included Hippocrates' emphasis on observation and clinical practice, which set the stage for future medical practices. Galen's extensive writings and experiments with animal anatomy synthesized knowledge from earlier scholars and established a framework for understanding human physiology that persisted throughout the Middle Ages and into the Renaissance. His work, particularly on the circulatory system, laid the groundwork for later discoveries by scientists like William Harvey in the 17th century, who would challenge Galen's theories and further advance the field.

The legacy of physiology is profound, influencing countless disciplines, including medicine, biology, and even philosophy. The transition from ancient to modern physiological understandings catalyzed the development of experimental methods in biology and medicine, shaping the scientific revolution and leading to significant advancements in healthcare. As physiology evolved, it became integral to the rise of modern medicine and public health initiatives, ultimately impacting global health standards and medical ethics in the contemporary era.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Physiology (from Greek φύσις, physis, 'nature', and λόγος, logos, 'study') is the branch of biology concerned with the normal functions and mechanisms of living organisms — the study of how cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems work together to maintain life, respond to the environment, and support vital processes including metabolism, respiration, circulation, digestion, neural signalling, reproduction, and homeostasis. Physiology is both an ancient and a modern discipline — its roots extend to Hippocratic and Galenic medicine (the humoral theory of physiological function that dominated Western medicine from antiquity to the 17th century) and its modern scientific form was established in the 17th–19th centuries through the work of William Harvey (discovery of blood circulation, 1628), René Descartes (mechanical model of the body), Albrecht von Haller (irritability and sensibility of tissues, 1750s), Claude Bernard (internal environment and homeostasis, 1850s–1860s), and the development of experimental physiology as an autonomous discipline.

Modern physiology is subdivided into numerous specialisms: cellular and molecular physiology (the function of individual cells and their molecular mechanisms), systems physiology (the function of organ systems — cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal, neurological, endocrine, reproductive), comparative physiology (comparing physiological mechanisms across different organisms), exercise physiology (the physiological responses to physical activity), and pathophysiology (the physiological mechanisms of disease). The boundaries between physiology and related disciplines — biochemistry, molecular biology, pharmacology, neuroscience, and medicine — are fluid and overlapping, reflecting physiology's position as the integrative discipline that links molecular mechanisms to whole-organism function.

The history of physiology is inseparable from the history of medicine — the understanding of how the body works in health is the foundation for understanding how it fails in disease, and physiological research has directly generated most of the major advances in clinical medicine: Harvey's circulation underpinning cardiovascular medicine, Bernard's homeostasis concept underpinning metabolic medicine and intensive care, and the discoveries of electrophysiology underpinning cardiology and neurology.
